findings.passage: Asked what she wants people to know about her, she ranked trust above liking:
findings.problem: The question is reworded, and the quote is put in the Six column. The evidence record (C134, S42 0:07-0:13) gives Buchanan's question as "What do you want people to know about this career that you're forging?" It was about her career, not about her as a person. The companion line makes the meaning plain. In Nylon (July 2026, opened 2026-10-22) the sentence between "lightning in a bottle" and "fall on my face publicly" is "I want people to take that time to trust that I have that capability." The draft's ending cuts exactly that sentence ("A few sentences later"). In context, "trust me" means trust my capability and career judgment. That is the credibility motive the draft assigns to Three elsewhere ("taken seriously", "prove myself"). Presenting it as a security-flavored ranking of trust over liking tilts a contested typing toward the leading read. Limitation: YouTube returned HTTP 429, so the Buchanan question wording rests on the evidence record's transcript; the Nylon wording was checked directly.
findings.acceptance_test: The passage says the question was about the career she is building (Kyle Buchanan Show, October 2026). The quote is either moved to the Three case or explicitly shown to cut both ways, citing Nylon's "trust that I have that capability" (July 2026). C134 is removed from type_hypothesis.for_claim_ids, or its inference is rewritten to reflect the career context. No sentence uses the line as evidence of a security motive without that context.

findings.passage: No episode on record yet forces those motives apart.
findings.problem: The draft leaves out the Heat 2 correction from the same Kyle Buchanan interview it relies on. Informed readers saw it widely reported (THR, 2026-10-21, opened 2026-10-22). Rumors said she turned down Heat 2 for X-Men. She volunteered the less flattering truth: "I'm glad that you brought it up because I can say it. No, I was not offered Heat 2." She said she auditioned for about two months and sent multiple self-tapes asking "What do you like? What do you not like?" She also said "I just wanted to learn" and "no matter how big you get, you're still gonna get told no." Research logged this as C127 and judged it "mildly against a Three reading that would let the flattering rumor stand." The draft dropped it, then states flatly that no episode separates the motives. It also lists such a career moment only as a future settle signal. The episode does not discriminate cleanly, because correcting the rumor also spares her from looking ungrateful to Michael Mann. It still belongs in the weighing. The self-tape questions also extend the draft's guide-seeking pattern (Chriqui, Barker).
findings.acceptance_test: The Six-vs-Three weighing includes the Heat 2 correction, dated and attributed (THR, October 21, 2026, relaying the Kyle Buchanan Show). It says what the episode suggests and what limits it (it is also image repair). The sentence "No episode on record yet forces those motives apart" is qualified to match. The alternative is a resolution that explains, with evidence, why the episode is excluded.

findings.passage: By 2026, after a hit, the cut had become a liberation.
findings.problem: The Superman & Lois exit is cropped, and the cropping favors the Seven-reframe reading. In the same Collider answer as "Dog, you're free" she said "that was hard to hear cuz I miss everybody," and framed the freedom as freedom to do film ("I've always wanted to do film... like I graduated"; evidence C12). In June 2026 (S37) she called it "disappointed and sad" as well as "divine timing" (C77). The evidence record itself says the article should weigh the freedom line against these (C12 alternative). The same Cinemablend TikTok quote the draft trims (opened 2026-10-22) also says she and others became "guest stars instead of series regulars, and so we'll be in about three episodes at least." She did not leave the show in 2023, which fans of the show know. A reframe that keeps the loss in view is weaker Seven evidence than the draft implies.
findings.acceptance_test: The passage keeps "Dog, you're free". It also includes, attributed and dated, her same-answer acknowledgment that it was "hard to hear" (Collider, May 2026) or the "disappointed and sad" line (June 2026). It notes that she stayed on as a guest star for Season 4. The Seven inference in the next sentence is tested against these lines, not against the freedom line alone.

findings.passage: She hosts _Saturday Night Live_ on October 31, 2026
findings.problem: The draft treats her post-Obsession record as empty in ways an informed reader will notice at once. First, it never mentions that she was cast as Rogue in Marvel's X-Men reboot (announced August 2026; THR gives a May 5, 2028 release). Yet two cited URLs carry "marvel-rogue" and "x-men-stunt-training" in their slugs. On Awards Chatter she tied Rogue to wanting "the freedom of being a completely different person" and "to not look like myself in some characters" (THR, opened 2026-10-22). That bears on the Three/Four reading and on her stated wish to be seen only on her own terms. Second, settle signal 3 asks for a future career choice and ignores the ones on record. Third, settle signal 2 and its FAQ ("or a run of real criticism") imply she has not yet been criticized. A September 2026 online pile-on was covered (S56). Its claims are unverified and should not be imported, but the signal should not read as if it never happened.
findings.acceptance_test: (a) The orientation paragraph has one dated sentence on the Rogue casting (announced August 2026; release dated May 5, 2028). It is recorded as a time_sensitive claim with a review trigger. (b) Settle signal 3 notes that the Rogue choice does not discriminate, because security and prestige point the same way. (c) Settle signal 2 and the matching FAQ answer are reworded, for example as "the first time she answers criticism on record". They must not describe the September 2026 posts or their allegations.

findings.passage: she thought, "I'm going to have so much fun with this, because who cares?"
findings.problem: The audition story is split across type columns, and each column gets only the half it can use. The Seven case gets the THR "who cares?" line. It does not get the line that follows it in the same answer: "You either have to send it or not go in at all." That reads as a deliberate push past doubt, not as ease. W (October 2026, opened 2026-10-22) says she "was convinced that she had been terrible": "on my second audition for Obsession, I just couldn't get there... it's not going to be me!" The draft quotes W's very next sentence ("my heart sank to my butt") for Six without that setup. On Awards Chatter, reading the script, she thought it would require "a lot of me that I don't know if I'm capable of," then told herself "Shut up, you are so capable of this." Fans of the W cover will recognize the doubt-bravado-despair sequence. Read whole, it weakens "who cares?" as standing Seven appetite.
findings.acceptance_test: The Seven paragraph places "who cares?" next to "send it or not go in at all" (THR, May 2026) and the W second-audition account (October 2026), both attributed. If it can't, it stops using "who cares?" as Seven evidence. The W "heart sank" quote is introduced with its setup: she had been sure she failed.

findings.passage: She knew the cost to him. "I know Curry's nervous," she said, and refusing him felt like "really being a dick."
findings.problem: The opening anecdote stops before its outcome as she told it. In the same Awards Chatter excerpt (THR, opened 2026-10-22) she goes on: "he'll even say now that it was a weight lifted off of his shoulders when we did that first freakout, because he was like, 'Oh my God, okay, she can do it! She just needs privacy with these things.'" Without that, the hook's puzzle is left as unresolved friction. The word "privacy" also links the most distinctive thread in her record: the withheld freakouts, "I don't like to be seen unless I want to be seen" (W), and watching her own film with audiences in disguise ("I hide really well, and they don't see me. I've worn many wigs," W). Co-star Michael Johnston also described her refusing to show him the freaky-Nikki smile ("Show me what you're going to do." ... "No."; Hot Ones Versus, S13). That is the only second witness to the pattern, but the evidence record says the speaker attribution still needs visual confirmation.
findings.acceptance_test: The freakout section includes the outcome she reports, attributed as her account of Barker's later view (THR Awards Chatter, October 2026), and does not present it as Barker's verified statement. Johnston's line is added only after the speaker is confirmed visually. Otherwise the evidence record notes why it is left out.

findings.passage: She has described those years at least four ways:
findings.problem: A section about how she tells her childhood leaves out its most striking variance and a disclosure she flagged as new. At TIFF in September 2026 she told ET, "I've never told this publicly... I have a divorced family. And I grew up in Texas for a good majority of my life," naming Corpus Christi (S47, machine transcript). She told Variety in July 2026 that her mother had the children live mostly around Fresno, Visalia and Bakersfield ("I love Visalia"). Wikipedia says she was raised mainly in Visalia (C113). Informed readers know she has given both answers, and the divorce helps explain the shuttling between places. Omitting both makes "Read together, they are a story about adapting" look tidier than her own accounts are.
findings.acceptance_test: The section adds one or two dated, attributed sentences: her parents' divorce, which she disclosed in September 2026, and the conflicting accounts of where she mostly grew up (Central Valley to Variety, Texas to ET). It makes no claim about psychological effect. The ET line is quoted only after the audio is checked; otherwise it is paraphrased with attribution. The alternative is a resolution that records why the material is excluded.

findings.passage: _Obsession_, in which a wish on a supernatural toy leaves her character, Nikki, obsessed with her co-worker Bear
findings.problem: The premise sentence doesn't say whose wish it is, and many readers will assume Nikki made it. In the film, Bear (Michael Johnston) makes the wish and Nikki is its object. Wikipedia (S29) has Bear's toy "grants his wish for his friend Nikki to fall in love with him." W calls Bear "a lovelorn man... who wishes on a magic willow stick that his crush, Nikki, will fall in love with him." THR describes her character as "a young woman whose free will is stolen by a friend's wish." The distinction matters to the portrait. She plays a woman whose will is overwritten, and she says Nikki taught her to stand up for herself (C33).
findings.acceptance_test: The premise sentence names Bear (Michael Johnston) as the one who makes the wish and Nikki as its object. Example: "in which her co-worker Bear's wish on a supernatural toy makes her character, Nikki, obsessed with him."

assessment: Fan-proxy read: the draft is candid about how thin the record is, avoids flattery, and is strongest when it lets her own contradictory words stand. The main weakness for an informed reader is selective cropping. Several well-known stories are cut at the point where they complicate the leading read. The "trust me" quote loses its career context and its Nylon companion sentence. The Superman & Lois exit loses "hard to hear" and her guest return. The audition loses the W account of being sure she failed. The freakout story loses its outcome. Meanwhile the post-Obsession record (the Rogue casting, the Heat 2 correction, the September 2026 criticism) is treated as empty, and fans will notice. None of this changes the open-case verdict. Two items (fan-01, fan-02) move evidence between the Six and Three columns and need weighing. Similarity advisory: I compared the tripped pairs. "Whose core emotion is fear" (Essiedu, Abbott, Beatty, Reiter) is ordinary type vocabulary. "Held loosely at low confidence" follows the open-case answer pattern the standard prescribes. The triad gloss closely parallels Ella Beatty's ("ground to trust in preparation, allies and the people in charge") but is orientation, not reused argument, so it is not raised as a finding. Tying it to her own words would still help. Sources opened 2026-10-22: THR Heat 2 (S43), THR Awards Chatter (S40), Cinemablend (S32), Nylon (S02), W (S44), Variety (S51). YouTube returned HTTP 429, so the Collider, Variety podcast, Complex, ET and Kyle Buchanan wording was checked only against the evidence record. Risks: contested_typing and major_thesis_change stand. sensitive_allegations stays false provided the September 2026 posts are not described.
